Family Health

Hemochromatosis: why iron builds up and how it is treated

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hemochromatosis involves too much iron accumulating in the body. Iron is essential, but the body has limited ways to remove a surplus. Over time, excess stores can damage organs. Many people have few noticeable symptoms at first, making appropriate testing and follow-up important when there is a family history or another reason to suspect iron overload.

What happens when the body stores too much iron?

Normally, the body adjusts how much iron it absorbs from food. When that control is disrupted, or iron repeatedly enters through transfusions, the amount stored can rise beyond what the body needs. This is a gradual problem in many cases, rather than something a person immediately feels.

Iron can collect in the liver, heart, pancreas, joints, skin and hormone-producing tissues, including the pituitary gland. Which tissues are affected, and how severely, helps determine the symptoms and treatment plan.

Hemochromatosis is often used to describe the inherited condition. The term secondary iron overload is useful when excess iron has another cause. These problems may have similar consequences, but their management is not always the same.

Symptoms may be absent or easy to attribute to something else

Some people are identified through family testing or an abnormal blood test before they feel unwell. When symptoms occur, they may include tiredness, weakness, unintentional weight loss, joint pain, abdominal discomfort or a reduced interest in sex.

Skin may become darker, sometimes with a bronze or grey appearance. Erectile difficulties or changes in menstrual patterns can develop if hormone function is affected. These findings are not unique to iron overload and do not establish a diagnosis on their own.

Describe persistent changes to a clinician, particularly if a close relative has hemochromatosis. Having no symptoms does not necessarily mean that iron levels are normal, while common symptoms such as fatigue can have many other explanations.

Inherited hemochromatosis and the HFE gene

The most common inherited form involves changes in HFE, a gene on chromosome 6 that helps regulate iron absorption. Two variants often discussed in test results are C282Y and H63D. They do not carry the same likelihood of clinically important disease.

The usual higher-risk pattern is inheriting a C282Y copy from each parent. A combination of C282Y and H63D is generally associated with a lower risk, and H63D alone usually has much less clinical significance. A specialist interprets the genetic result together with iron tests and the person’s health.

Even people who inherit a higher-risk combination do not all develop harmful iron overload. Genetic susceptibility, test evidence of extra iron and organ damage are different findings. Other health conditions and environmental factors can influence how the condition develops.

This common HFE-related form is more frequent in people with northern European ancestry, but ancestry should not be used to dismiss an unexplained test result. Rarer inherited iron disorders also exist and may require a different assessment.

Why symptoms can appear later in women

Men and women can inherit the relevant variants, but clinical problems from iron overload are more often recognized in men. Menstrual blood loss removes some iron, which can delay its accumulation. Women may therefore first develop symptoms after menopause.

This is an average pattern, not a rule that protects every person who menstruates or excludes the condition in a younger adult. Family history, iron results and symptoms remain relevant at any appropriate age.

Diabetes or liver disease may coexist with iron overload or reflect damage from it. Their presence can affect the assessment, but neither condition by itself proves hemochromatosis.

Other reasons for iron overload

Repeated blood transfusions can add more iron than the body can remove. This can happen in people who need ongoing transfusions for severe anaemia, including some people with thalassaemia, sickle cell disease or bone-marrow disorders.

Some red-cell disorders also disturb iron regulation. The explanation is more complex than simply saying that fragile red cells release too much iron: ineffective blood-cell production, increased absorption and transfusion history may all matter.

Iron accumulation can also occur with certain liver diseases. Alcohol misuse can contribute to liver injury and worsen iron-related problems. Excessive iron supplements or injections are another possible source of overload.

Vitamin C increases iron absorption, so concentrated supplements deserve particular discussion when iron is already high. Ordinary foods containing vitamin C do not require an automatic ban. A family history of heart disease, diabetes or liver disease is useful clinical information, but is not itself a cause of secondary iron overload.

How the assessment begins

A clinician will ask about your symptoms, medicines and supplements, previous transfusions, alcohol use, medical history and relatives with hemochromatosis or related health problems. Bringing supplement labels or a medication list can make this easier.

The examination may include checking the abdomen, skin and joints. Because fatigue, pain and other symptoms overlap with many conditions, the clinician combines this information with tests rather than diagnosing from appearance or symptoms alone.

Tell the clinician if you are planning pregnancy or if a relative has a confirmed genetic result. These details may affect advice about family testing, supplements and referral.

Blood tests: iron transport, storage and organ function

Transferrin is the protein that transports iron in the blood. Transferrin saturation describes how much of its iron-carrying capacity is occupied. Ferritin helps assess stored iron. Both can be useful, rather than relying on a single blood-iron measurement.

A full blood count and liver blood tests may also be included. Results are interpreted together and in context; an abnormal iron-related result does not automatically identify the inherited cause.

If the initial findings suggest iron overload, further tests or a specialist assessment can establish the cause and whether treatment is needed. Ask which results are being followed and when they should be repeated.

Genetic testing and advice for relatives

Testing can identify HFE variants or, in selected cases, other inherited causes. It generally uses a blood sample, although the laboratory may accept a cheek-swab sample for some DNA tests.

A close family history is a reason to discuss testing even without symptoms. Genetic counselling can explain what a result means for you and relatives, and can help with questions before having children. Testing is an informed clinical decision, not an automatic requirement for everyone planning a pregnancy.

A result showing a variant does not on its own measure current organ damage or determine the need for blood removal. The clinician considers iron levels and the type of variant. Advice on testing children also differs from advice for adult relatives, particularly when the usual condition starts in adulthood.

MRI and liver biopsy have different roles

The liver is an important iron-storage organ and can be affected early. A liver MRI may help quantify iron without removing tissue. Other noninvasive assessments can help evaluate liver scarring or particular organ problems.

A liver biopsy takes a small tissue sample for laboratory examination. It can assess iron and liver damage, and help answer questions about other liver disease. It is not necessary for everyone with suspected hemochromatosis.

The specialist chooses the appropriate tests based on what remains uncertain. MRI can sometimes avoid a biopsy, but the two are not interchangeable in every situation.

Phlebotomy removes iron through controlled blood removal

For many people with inherited iron overload, the main treatment is phlebotomy, also called venesection. A needle is placed in a vein and blood is collected in a bag, in a process similar to blood donation. Removing red cells removes iron; replacing those cells then draws on stored iron.

A session often removes roughly a pint, or about 500 mL, but the amount and frequency are prescribed individually. Early treatment may involve weekly sessions, sometimes more frequently, until excess stores have fallen. This can take months and occasionally longer.

Once iron is controlled, treatment usually becomes less frequent. Some people attend every few months or a few times a year. Regular blood tests guide both phases; treatment should not continue on a fixed timetable regardless of the results or how well it is tolerated.

Do not arrange repeated blood donation as a substitute for assessment. Anaemia, heart problems or other circumstances may change what is safe. Whether collected blood can be donated also depends on the blood service’s rules.

Chelation is an alternative for selected situations

Chelation medicines bind iron so it can leave the body in urine or stool. Depending on the medicine, treatment may be taken by mouth or given by injection or infusion. It is an established approach to some forms of iron overload, rather than simply an experimental version of blood removal.

It is particularly relevant when a person still needs transfusions for anaemia and cannot safely have blood removed. It may also be considered in other circumstances where regular phlebotomy is unsuitable. The choice depends on the cause of overload and the person’s overall condition.

Chelation can be more complex and costly, and medicines require monitoring for adverse effects. Possible problems differ between drugs and routes of administration; injection-site reactions are relevant to injected treatments, while feeling feverish or unwell needs advice rather than being dismissed as an expected reaction.

Ask the prescribing team about the specific medicine, monitoring, interactions and symptoms that should prompt contact. Do not use a supplement or a commercially promoted “detox” treatment as an alternative.

Complications depend on which organs are affected

Untreated iron overload can cause liver damage and scarring. Severe liver disease may require transplant assessment, and cirrhosis increases the risk of liver cancer. Lowering iron does not remove every consequence of established liver disease.

Damage to the pancreas can contribute to diabetes. Joint damage may cause persistent arthritis-like pain. Iron in the heart can affect its rhythm or pumping ability and lead to heart failure.

Skin pigmentation can change, and hormone problems can affect sexual function or periods. The endocrine assessment may include pituitary or other gland function; adrenal problems should be investigated when clinically suspected, rather than assumed to affect everyone with hemochromatosis.

Early diagnosis, iron control and treatment of any complications can reduce harm. Persistent joint pain, diabetes or other established problems may still need separate care even when iron levels improve.

Everyday care supports, but does not replace, treatment

Attend follow-up and keep a record of iron results, treatment dates and symptoms. The testing interval depends on the treatment phase and stability of the condition; an annual check is not enough for everyone, especially during frequent blood removal.

Discuss every supplement with the care team. Iron and vitamin C supplements are usually avoided when iron is high, including multivitamins that contain them. Do not stop a prescribed treatment or remove all vitamins from your diet without discussing your situation.

Aim for a balanced diet rather than eliminating all iron-containing foods. Food changes alone have a much smaller effect on excess iron stores than treatment. Seek individual advice if you also have diabetes, liver disease or other nutritional needs.

Alcohol advice depends partly on liver health. Avoid heavy drinking and follow the clinician’s limits; complete avoidance is advised with cirrhosis. If stopping alcohol may cause withdrawal, arrange medical support.

Take infection prevention seriously, including suitable vaccinations and good hygiene. Avoid raw or undercooked shellfish, which can cause particularly serious infection in people with liver disease or high iron levels.

Report new or worsening symptoms and explain how fatigue, pain or sexual difficulties affect daily life. A normalizing blood result should not end the conversation about ongoing symptoms or quality of life.

What the long-term outlook can be

The outlook is often good when the condition is recognized and treated before significant organ damage. Many people can expect a normal lifespan with appropriate treatment and continued monitoring.

Reducing iron can improve some symptoms and prevent further injury, but it cannot be promised to reverse every problem already present. Liver scarring, diabetes or joint damage may require continuing treatment and surveillance.

Hereditary susceptibility remains even after iron stores fall. Maintenance care and appropriate advice for relatives help manage that ongoing risk without assuming that every relative will become ill.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance distinguishes blood tests for iron storage and transport from genetic testing and investigations for organ damage. A family diagnosis is a reason to discuss assessment even when symptoms are absent.

NIDDK advises treatment directed at the cause of iron overload and a balanced diet. Restrictive diets cannot replace prescribed iron removal, and established organ damage may not fully reverse.

How BeMama can help

BeMama provides general education to help you prepare for a health appointment. Use the questions here to discuss test results, supplements, family history and follow-up. BeMama cannot interpret a genetic result, prescribe blood removal or monitor iron levels.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment for persistent unexplained symptoms or a close relative with hemochromatosis. Seek urgent care for severe chest pain, serious breathing difficulty, collapse or another sudden severe illness. If treatment causes new symptoms, contact the treating team for advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Iron overload may be present before noticeable symptoms develop.
  • Inherited HFE-related disease and secondary iron overload can need different treatment.
  • Genetic susceptibility does not guarantee organ damage; blood results and clinical findings matter.
  • Phlebotomy or chelation requires an individualized plan and monitoring.
  • Early treatment can prevent harm, but established damage may not fully reverse.

Frequently asked questions

Does a high iron result mean I inherited hemochromatosis?

Not necessarily. The clinician considers transferrin saturation, ferritin, other tests and possible causes such as transfusions, liver disease or excess supplements. Genetic testing may help clarify the cause.

If I have an HFE variant, will I definitely become ill?

No. Risk depends on the variant combination and other factors. Some people have genetic susceptibility without significant iron overload or organ damage.

Should relatives be tested before they have symptoms?

A close family diagnosis is a reason to ask about testing. A clinician or genetics service can advise which relatives to assess and when, including how recommendations differ for children and adults.

Will I need a liver biopsy?

Not always. Blood tests and noninvasive investigations, including MRI in selected cases, may answer the relevant questions. A specialist explains whether a biopsy would add useful information.

Can I treat this just by changing what I eat?

Diet alone is not a substitute for prescribed treatment. A balanced diet, supplement review and appropriate alcohol advice support care without requiring you to avoid every food containing iron.

Can I stop treatment once my levels are normal?

Do not stop independently. Many people with inherited iron overload need maintenance treatment and blood tests. The frequency is adjusted to their results and tolerance.

Does treatment reverse all the damage?

It can improve some symptoms and prevent further injury, especially when started early. Established scarring, diabetes or joint problems may persist and need separate care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
